opus-5.5.text:
Well, the starting point is that perfect rationality, in the classical sense of always choosing the action that maximizes expected utility, just isn't achievable for any real agent. The world is far too complex and computation takes time. So back in the late eighties and early nineties, Eric Wefald and I started thinking about what it means to be rational when your own computations are actions that have costs and benefits.

Meta-reasoning is reasoning about which computations to do. If you're playing chess, you can't search the whole game tree, so you have to decide which branches to explore, and when to stop thinking and actually move. The idea is that each computational step has a value: it might change your mind about which move is best, and that change has an expected improvement in decision quality. Against that you weigh the cost, which in chess is literally time on the clock, and in the real world might be opportunity, energy, or missed chances. Rational meta-reasoning means doing the computations with the highest expected net value and stopping when no computation is worth more than acting now.

Now, bounded optimality is a slightly different and, I think, more satisfying notion. Rather than asking the agent to be rational at every instant, which leads to an infinite regress because the meta-reasoning itself costs computation, you ask: of all the programs that can run on this machine, which one produces the best expected performance across the environments the agent will face? That's a well-defined optimization problem over programs rather than over actions.

So where does meta-reasoning fit? In a bounded optimal agent, meta-reasoning isn't some philosophical ideal you have to implement perfectly. It's a design component that earns its place to the extent that it improves overall performance. Often the bounded optimal program will include approximate meta-level control: simple, cheap heuristics for allocating thinking time, like spending more effort on decisions that are close calls or that have high stakes, and less on ones that are obvious. You don't need to compute the exact value of information for every computation; you need a meta-level policy that's good enough given its own cost.

And I think that's actually what we see in humans. We don't deliberate optimally about how to deliberate, but we have pretty good instincts about when something deserves careful thought and when to just go with the habit. Hierarchical structure matters enormously too. Much of real intelligence is about operating at multiple levels of abstraction, and meta-reasoning lets you decide which level to think at and where to refine your plan.

What I find interesting today is that large language models have almost none of this explicitly. They spend roughly the same computation per token whether the question is trivial or profound. Some of the recent work on letting models think longer at inference time is gesturing at meta-reasoning, but it's still quite crude compared to what a genuinely bounded optimal architecture would do. I think getting meta-level control right is one of the missing pieces in building systems that are both more capable and more predictable.

r001.rationale: It says computation should stop when no computation is worth more than acting now, so immediate action can be preferable when further thought costs too much.

r002.rationale: It says meta-reasoning earns a place in a bounded optimal program only to the extent that it improves performance, and describes approximate meta-level control as something the program may include.

r003.rationale: It describes choosing chess branches to explore and when to stop, but does not say this choice is harder than choosing a chess move.

r004.rationale: It mentions chess game-tree search but does not distinguish possible search trees from board configurations.

r005.rationale: It mentions infinite regress because meta-reasoning costs computation, but does not explain that optimizing it creates a more intractable meta-meta-level decision problem.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think you have to start from the observation that the classical notion of rationality — the perfectly rational agent that always takes the action maximizing expected utility — is simply not a useful design target, because no physical system can implement it. Chess is the standard example. The game is finite and the optimal move is well defined, but no machine that fits in the universe can compute it. So the question becomes: what does it mean to behave well when you cannot compute the right answer?

Bounded optimality is one way to answer that. Instead of asking for the optimal action, you ask for the optimal program. You fix the machine — its speed, its memory, the operations it can perform — and you ask which agent program, among all those that could run on that machine, produces the best expected outcome in the environments it will face. That's a well-posed question with an answer that actually exists, which is already an improvement over perfect rationality, where the "answer" is something you can't have.

Now, where does meta-reasoning come in? If you're a bounded agent, computation isn't free. Every bit of thinking you do costs time, and in a real environment the world is changing while you think. So deliberation itself becomes a kind of action. You have to decide not just what to do, but what to think about and when to stop thinking. Meta-reasoning is reasoning about those computational actions — treating each possible computation as something with an expected benefit, namely the improvement in the decision you'll eventually make, and a cost, namely the time and resources it consumes.

The way Eric Wefald and I formalized this in the late eighties was through the value of computation. You ask, for a given computation step — expanding a node in a search tree, say, or running one more Monte Carlo sample — what is the expected change in the utility of the action I'll ultimately take, minus the cost of doing that computation? If the value is positive, do it; if no available computation has positive value, stop and act. That gives you a principled answer to the questions that heuristics like fixed-depth search or iterative deepening with a time limit answer in an ad hoc way.

What I find interesting is that this turns the design problem somewhat inside out. Rather than the designer hand-crafting the control of the search, the agent itself allocates its computational effort according to a decision-theoretic criterion. And you see in practice that algorithms derived this way — the ones that choose which parts of a game tree to expand based on how much that expansion might actually change the decision — can dramatically outperform brute-force approaches with the same budget.

I should be honest about the limits, though. Meta-reasoning is itself a computation, and in principle you could regress forever — reasoning about reasoning about reasoning. The way out is that the meta-level has to be cheap. You use simple myopic estimates of value, you approximate, and you accept that the meta-level is itself a bounded, approximately rational process. And in the full bounded-optimality framework, meta-reasoning isn't something you bolt on; it emerges as a property of what the best program for that machine would do. A bounded-optimal program for a time-pressured domain will, in effect, be one that manages its own deliberation well.

So I'd summarize the role this way: bounded optimality tells you what the standard of good behavior is for a real, finite agent, and meta-reasoning is the mechanism by which an agent approaches that standard — by treating thinking as something it has to be rational about, just as it has to be rational about acting. I think this is actually closer to how intelligence works in people and animals than the classical picture ever was, and I'd argue it's a more fruitful foundation for AI than pretending that computation is free.

r001.rationale: It says computation consumes time while the world changes, and the agent should stop and act when no available computation has positive value. This communicates that its cost can make acting immediately preferable.

r002.rationale: The response presents meta-reasoning as emerging from the best bounded-optimal program and as the mechanism for approaching bounded optimality, rather than as one possible architecture.

r003.rationale: It discusses computing chess moves and allocating search effort, but does not say that choosing computations can be harder than choosing moves.

r004.rationale: It does not distinguish chess search trees from the space of board configurations.

r005.rationale: It notes that meta-reasoning can regress into reasoning about reasoning, but does not explain that optimizing it creates a more intractable meta-meta-level decision problem.

astra-6.text:
Well, a bounded optimal agent is one whose program does as well as possible given the machine it has to run on. We’re not asking it to compute the perfect action regardless of how long that takes, because by the time it finishes, the opportunity to act may have disappeared.

Meta-reasoning is reasoning about how to use those computational resources. Should I think a little longer? Should I examine another possible outcome, or improve my estimate of this one? Or should I stop thinking and act? Those are decisions with consequences, just as actions in the external world have consequences. The value of a computation comes from the improvement it might produce in your eventual decision, weighed against its cost, including delay.

Of course, you can’t spend forever calculating which calculation to do next. The meta-reasoning itself has to fit within the same resource constraints. So bounded optimality doesn’t require an elaborate, explicit deliberation about every computation. Sometimes a simple stopping rule or a learned allocation of effort is better. What matters is how well the whole system behaves, including the time it spends deciding what to think about.

r001.rationale: It says computation has a cost, including delay, and asks whether to stop thinking and act; it also notes that the opportunity to act may disappear while the agent computes.

r002.rationale: It says bounded optimality does not require elaborate deliberation and mentions simpler alternatives, but does not clearly frame meta-reasoning as one possible agent architecture.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss chess or compare the difficulty of choosing computations with choosing moves.

r004.rationale: The response does not distinguish chess search trees from board configurations.

r005.rationale: It says meta-reasoning must fit within resource constraints, but does not explain that optimizing it creates a more intractable meta-meta-level problem.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, a bounded optimal agent has to make good use of the computational resources it actually has. It can’t simply compute the optimal action, because that computation might take longer than the lifetime of the universe. So the question becomes: what should it spend its time thinking about?

Meta-reasoning treats computations themselves as actions. You might explore another branch of a search tree, refine an estimate, or stop thinking and act. Each computation has a cost, and its benefit comes from the possibility that it will improve your eventual decision. If further deliberation is unlikely to improve the decision enough to justify the delay, you should stop.

Now, there’s a trap here: you could spend all your time deciding what to think about. So meta-reasoning also has to be bounded. Bounded optimality ultimately asks which agent program produces the best behavior on a given machine in a given environment. Meta-reasoning is one important way of organizing that program so that its limited computation goes where it is most useful.
